a: The most isolated inhabited place on Earth is generally considered to be Tristan da Cunha, a volcanic island in the South Atlantic Ocean. Located roughly 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) west of Cape Town, South Africa, and 3,360 kilometers (2,090 miles) east of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, it is the most remote permanently inhabited island in the world. The island has about 250 year-round residents who live in the settlement of Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. Supplies arrive only every six weeks by ship from Cape Town, and the nearest other inhabited land is over 2,000 kilometers away. Other extremely isolated inhabited places include Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in the Pacific, famous for its moai statues with around 7,700 residents, and Pitcairn Island with only about 50 residents. While Tristan da Cunha holds the record for the greatest distance from any other human settlement, Greenland and the remote islands of the Faroe archipelago, Svalbard, and St. Helena are also among the world's most isolated inhabited territories.
